what_it_does: Large language models (the kind that power AI chat tools) store billions of numerical weights, and keeping those weights as full 16-bit floating-point numbers demands huge amounts of memory and bandwidth. Quantization — rounding those weights to smaller, cruder numbers — saves space, but a handful of unusually large 'outlier' values resist rounding and cause accuracy to drop. PISA addresses this by splitting each 16-bit value into two parts: a compact 4-bit slice that holds the most important information and a 12-bit slice for the remainder. Because the higher-order bits of most values are mostly zeros, those bits are sparse (they can be skipped), making the 12-bit slice cheap to process. An 'early bird' mechanism goes further: it runs computation on just the 4-bit slice first, decides whether the result is important enough to bother refining with the 12-bit slice, and skips the full computation when it isn't. The design is built to slot into systolic arrays — the grid of small multiplier units that AI accelerator chips commonly use — without requiring a complete hardware redesign.
